stories.headline: Tesco Accused of Concealing Forced Labor at Thai Factory as UK Lawsuit Advances
stories.claim: Tesco faces a UK High Court lawsuit over alleged forced labour at a Thai supplier, with a new report alleging it concealed abuses.
stories.summary: Former Burmese migrant workers, represented by Leigh Day, are suing Tesco and auditor Intertek in the UK High Court over conditions at V.K. Garment in Mae Sot, Thailand, where they made jeans and jackets for Tesco's F&F clothing line between 2017 and 2020. The claimants describe debt bondage, very long hours, unsafe conditions and, in one case, the rape of a seven-year-old child by a factory employee. Proceedings were first issued in 2022. A Worker Rights Consortium report published this week says Tesco and Intertek were aware of violations from a 2017 audit and that the audits omitted forced labour evidence. Tesco says it only learned of the abuses after selling its Thai subsidiary in 2020 and would have ended the relationship had it known. Intertek did not respond to the report's claims.
key_points: The claimants are 130 former Burmese migrant workers and one child, suing in the UK High Court.
The workers say they were trapped in debt bondage and worked up to 99 hours a week at V.K. Garment, Thailand.
The Worker Rights Consortium says Tesco's 2017 audit found withheld passports and missing work permits, yet production continued.
The report alleges the audits omitted evidence of forced labour and that factory records were fabricated.
Tesco says it did not know of the abuses until after selling its Thai subsidiary in 2020 and denies managing the supplier's daily operations.
The case is ongoing; no court ruling has been reported.
stories.market_take: Reputational and legal risk for Tesco and Intertek, though the financial impact is likely to be limited for now.

stocks.reason: Lawsuit and report raise reputational and potential legal risk around supply-chain oversight.

stories.summary: Macau casino operator Galaxy Entertainment Group reported unaudited results for the three months to 30 September 2026, with figures in Hong Kong dollars. Group net revenue reached HK$12.7 billion, up 4% year-on-year, and adjusted EBITDA rose 10% to HK$3.7 billion. Macau visitor arrivals were about 11.2 million, up 8% year-on-year, while market gaming revenue fell 4% to HK$58.5 billion for the quarter. Management said growth had moderated near term, citing factors including possible tax policy changes, slower global growth and geopolitical uncertainty, but remained confident in the medium term. The company also highlighted premium product expansion, entertainment events and a planned Phase 4 development.
key_points: Q3 2026 net revenue was HK$12.7 billion, up 4% year-on-year and 7% quarter-on-quarter.
Adjusted EBITDA was HK$3.7 billion, up 10% year-on-year.
Macau gross gaming revenue for Q3 was HK$58.5 billion, down 4% year-on-year.
Macau visitor arrivals reached about 11.2 million, up 8% year-on-year, with mainland arrivals up 10%.
Galaxy paid an interim dividend of HK$0.90 per share in September; cash and liquid investments were HK$36.4 billion.
StarWorld Macau renovation is targeted for completion in Q1 2027, and Phase 4 fit-out continues.
stories.market_take: Solid quarterly profit growth but moderating Macau gaming market may weigh on sentiment for casino stocks.

stories.headline: Pete Hegseth strikes defiant tone in face of impeachment threat

stories.claim: Invasive pasture mealybugs are damaging grass and crops across Texas, Louisiana, Georgia and Florida, with costs for farmers estimated in billions.

Approved pesticides exist but none is a complete solution and they are expensive, so researchers are studying the pest and crop resistance.

stories.summary: US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday declaring the Oval Office and some surrounding rooms a national monument. The order asks the National Park Service to maintain the space to protect its historic character, though it allows the president to redecorate and make ordinary security changes. Trump said the move would stop anyone from destroying the room, and described the White House as badly damaged before his changes. Critics, including preservation lawyer Greg Werkheiser, called the order hypocritical given Trump's other projects in Washington. The move follows the demolition of the East Wing for a ballroom project.

The order allows the president to redecorate and make ordinary operational or security changes.

The order comes days after Republicans lost ground in the midterm elections.

stories.headline: Get root on a musl Linux system by slamming it with an overly long password
stories.claim: A flaw in OpenSSH on certain musl-based Linux systems lets attackers reach no-password accounts; it is now fixed in version 10.6p2.
stories.summary: Security researcher Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield disclosed a vulnerability in OpenSSH, dubbed *sshole, that can let an attacker gain access to accounts that should not accept passwords, including root, by submitting a password between 257 and 1,024 characters. It only affects a narrow set of systems: those using the musl C library, running OpenSSH without PAM, with password authentication enabled, and with at least one account holding a valid password hash. The root cause dates to a 2016 change and traces back to an asterisk convention from early BSD Unix. OpenSSH build 10.6p2, released Thursday, fixes the issue. Alpine Linux images on AWS and Azure may be affected depending on configuration. There is no sign of exploitation so far.

stories.headline: HMRC bank account raid powers spark concern over burden of proof
stories.claim: HMRC will gain powers from July 2029 to take tax debts directly from bank accounts, announced in the Budget.

The powers would apply to debts up to £5,000 for individuals and up to £10,000 for companies, and take effect from July 2029. Current rules only allow recovery for debts above £1,000 and require at least £5,000 to remain in the account. The government expects the measures to raise £50m in the first year, £255m in 2030/31 and £320m in 2031/32, against a tax gap of £59.2bn in 2024/25. Accountants have raised concerns about affordability checks, disputed debts and how quickly errors can be reversed. HMRC says it will act only after repeated contact attempts. Separately, HMRC is pressing LLPs to reassess members' tax status after a July Supreme Court ruling in the BlueCrest case.

The findings will be published alongside a 5 November index update.

stories.headline: How Abdul El-Sayed would build Medicare for All, from a wealth tax to a Fed-style governing board
stories.claim: Abdul El-Sayed, who won Michigan's Senate race, lays out how he would build Medicare for All and its financing.
stories.summary: Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's open Senate race on a night when Democrats won both chambers of Congress. He is a leading advocate of Medicare for All, a single-payer system he co-wrote about in a 2021 book with Micah Johnson. The plan would cover physician visits, prescriptions and emergency care, possibly long-term care, vision and dental, and would be governed by a body insulated from the executive branch, similar to the Federal Reserve. Financing would combine existing federal spending with a wealth tax, a new corporate tax code and higher investment income taxes. Critics, including drug companies and the American Hospital Association, point to a 2018 estimate of $32.6 trillion in added federal spending over ten years for Sanders' version of the plan.

El-Sayed has said he would hope to avoid raising taxes on most Michigan families, including those earning around $100,000 a year, though experts think some middle-class increases would be needed.
Critics say the plan's cost is high; a 2018 analysis of Sanders' proposal estimated $32.6 trillion in extra federal spending over a decade.

stories.headline: Food prices in Europe: Where are grocery costs rising fastest?
stories.claim: Eurozone food inflation is rising unevenly, with unprocessed food up sharply in October and southern Italy's lorry-driver blockade emptying shelves.
stories.summary: Eurostat's preliminary data show eurozone inflation hit 4% in October, the highest in over three years, driven mainly by energy costs up 20.8%. Food, alcohol and tobacco rose 1.6% year on year, but unprocessed food such as fruit, vegetables, meat and fish climbed 4.6%, up from 2.7% in August. Italy saw unprocessed food up 7.5%, and a two-week lorry-driver protest over diesel costs in late October emptied shelves across Campania, Puglia and Calabria. France's fresh products rose 8%, while Germany's food rose only 0.4%. Economists expect inflation to keep climbing, with Pantheon Macroeconomics forecasting a peak of 4.5% in January and a possible ECB rate rise in December.

Sweden's food prices fell 6.3% in September after a VAT cut on food to 6% from April.
Pantheon Macroeconomics expects eurozone inflation to peak at 4.5% in January and the ECB to raise rates in December.

stories.headline: Albanese government warned it is ‘sleepwalking into another robodebt scenario’ over use of algorithms and AI
stories.claim: Australian think tank warns government is sleepwalking into a robodebt-style scandal over unregulated algorithmic decision-making.
stories.summary: The Centre for Public Integrity, an Australian independent thinktank, released a report titled Computer Says No warning that the federal government risks repeating the robodebt scandal because of weak transparency and no legislation governing automated decision-making (ADM). The report points to an algorithm in the government's integrated assessment tool, which assesses home care entitlements for older Australians and has been found to routinely under-assess needs. The thinktank makes eight recommendations, including a mandatory audit and public register of all ADM use and an independent oversight body. The attorney general's department has been developing an ADM framework since consultation ended in January 2025, but no draft date has been given. An independent MP, Kate Chaney, has also introduced a private member's bill on the issue.

stories.headline: Nintendo's biggest ROM chip supplier is bowing out of the business
stories.claim: Macronix, a major supplier of ROM chips, is ending ROM production, which could raise costs for Nintendo Switch game cartridges.
stories.summary: Taiwanese chipmaker Macronix said in its third-quarter earnings that production of ROM chips has reached its end and that it will gradually leave the game industry. ROM output has fallen 39 percent over the past year and is now only 5 percent of its business, as capacity shifts to more profitable NOR, NAND and eMMC chips. Analyst David Gibson says Nintendo relies on Macronix as its main memory supplier for physical cartridges. Nintendo said last month that it has no plans to abandon cartridges, but it may have to turn to suppliers such as Rohm and Lapis Semiconductor, which could raise costs. Digital sales were 61.5 percent of Nintendo's business in the second calendar quarter of 2026.

stories.headline: Scare campaigns: Victoria’s major parties trade blows over AI-generated videos of leaders in election ads
stories.claim: Victorian parties in Australia are trading AI-generated deepfake election ads, prompting calls for a ban and tighter rules.
stories.summary: In the run-up to the Victorian state election in Australia, the Labor and Liberal parties have both used AI-generated videos of their leaders in campaign material. A Labor video showed Liberal leader Jess Wilson with a fabricated voice warning of US-style healthcare costs, which her party called garbage. The Liberals have posted AI videos of Premier Ben Carroll asleep at his desk. A conservative lobby group, Advance Australia, also released an AI video depicting a fake Labor victory. Experts and the Greens are calling for AI in political ads to be banned, and Transparency International Australia says trust in politicians is at an all-time low. South Australia already bans deepfakes that show people doing things they did not do without consent, with fines of up to A$5,000.

stories.headline: Hackers used Chrome and Snapdragon GPU flaws to hack Android phones
stories.claim: Sekoia reports a mobile hacking campaign using Chrome and Qualcomm GPU flaws, already patched, targeting Android and iPhone users.
stories.summary: Security firm Sekoia has detailed a mobile hacking campaign targeting Android and iPhone users via hijacked and fake websites. On Android, opening an infected page in an outdated version of Chrome was enough to start the attack, which chained a Chrome flaw (CVE-2026-3910) with a Qualcomm Adreno GPU driver flaw (CVE-2025-27038) to escape the browser sandbox. Phones using Snapdragon chips were affected, and the Android exploit reportedly stopped if it detected a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. The attackers compromised a Ukrainian web analytics service and built lookalike sites, including one imitating a London luxury hotel near UK government offices. All the flaws had already been patched before the attacks began, so users are advised to update Chrome and their monthly security patches.

Snapdragon-powered phones were the affected devices; the exploit reportedly skipped Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra handsets.
Attackers compromised a Ukrainian web analytics service used by mostly Ukrainian sites between 27 August and 3 September.
All flaws were already patched; users should update Chrome to a version newer than 145 and install monthly security updates.

stories.headline: GSMA warns of growing risks to mobile networks from extreme weather
stories.claim: GSMA says extreme weather costs mobile operators $1.7bn a year, possibly rising above $3bn by 2050, and urges coordinated resilience.
stories.summary: The GSMA, the global mobile industry body, has published a six-part research series and a policy document on how extreme weather threatens mobile networks. It estimates that severe storms and floods already cost operators $1.7 billion a year to repair cell sites, a figure it expects could nearly double to more than $3 billion annually by 2050. The report identifies electricity supply as the biggest vulnerability, since networks can go offline once backup power runs out. It calls for operators, governments, regulators and energy providers to coordinate, and for policy frameworks that are outcome-based rather than prescriptive.
key_points: Severe storms and floods already cost mobile operators about $1.7 billion a year to repair cell radio sites.
The GSMA projects this could rise to more than $3 billion a year by 2050.

Recommendations include resilience by design, cross-sector testing and coordination among operators, utilities and emergency services.
Policy principles favour outcome-based regulation and consultation between governments and operators.
Barriers include internal data silos and differing regulatory and climate-disclosure frameworks.
stories.market_take: Mainly a policy and industry report; little direct effect on listed telecom shares.

stories.claim: Russia's communications regulator added Apple and Microsoft to a register requiring data retention and disclosure to security agencies.
stories.summary: Russia's communications regulator, Roskomnadzor, added Apple and Microsoft to an official register of digital communication providers on 2 October 2026, according to Bloomberg. The listing obliges the companies to store customer details and communication records within Russia for three years and to provide them to authorities on request. Firms that break the rules face fines and, if violations persist, possible service bans. Google Meet, WhatsApp, Telegram, Snapchat and others are already on the register. Apple has faced a series of disputes with Russia, including restrictions on App Store payments, removal of apps and an antitrust case over preinstalling state-backed software. Neither company has publicly said how it will respond.

stories.headline: Rapid LLM development is outrunning the research meant to explain it, study finds
stories.claim: A Stanford study finds 44% of widely cited LLM research claims have expired as newer models outpace earlier findings.
stories.summary: Stanford researchers Owen Queen and James Zou tested 50 widely cited claims about large language models against 20 models released between July 2024 and September 2026. They found 44% of the claims had expired, and the 22 findings with an estimated expiry lasted an average of 15.7 months. Claims about what models cannot do expire fastest, including known weaknesses such as counting letters or losing information in long contexts. Findings about preferences and tendencies, such as political bias and sycophancy, have proven more durable. Citation fabrication has fallen sharply in some models, but one 2026 model still fabricated 69% of references. The researchers urge papers to document the specific model, version and date, and to publish prompts and code so results can be re-tested.
key_points: The study tested 50 widely cited LLM claims against 20 models released from July 2024 to September 2026.
44% of claims have expired, 34% have weakened significantly, and 16% still hold.

Claims about model limitations, especially reasoning weaknesses, expire fastest.

stories.headline: Google AI chatbot’s use of press items may infringe copyright rules, EU court adviser says
stories.claim: EU Court of Justice adviser says Google's Gemini chatbot may infringe press publishers' copyright in certain circumstances.
stories.summary: Advocate General Maciej Szpunar, adviser to the EU's top court in Luxembourg, said that Google's Gemini chatbot can infringe press publishers' rights in some cases. This applies when it accesses articles by circumventing paywalls or reuses their expression in a recognisable way. He said copyright does not protect mere facts, and that training AI models on copyrighted text is freely permitted under the text and data mining exception. The case was brought by Hungarian website operator Like Company. Opinions of the advocate general are not binding but are usually followed by judges.
key_points: The case was brought by Hungarian website operator Like Company against Google over Gemini.
Szpunar said chatbot answers can infringe publishers' rights if paywalls are bypassed or expression is reused recognisably.
Facts reported in press articles are not protected by copyright, only their specific form of expression.
Training LLMs on copyrighted material is freely permitted under the EU text and data mining exception, according to the adviser.
Publishers say AI summaries are reducing traffic to their sites.
The advisory opinion is not binding, but the Court's judges usually follow it; a final ruling is still to come.
stories.market_take: A final ruling against Google could add licensing costs for AI search features.

stocks.name: Alphabet
stocks.reason: A ruling requiring payments for press content could raise Gemini's costs.

stories.headline: British fintech Revolut slashes AI coding costs 10x by cutting out Claude and going self-hosted
stories.claim: Revolut says switching most AI coding to self-hosted open-weight models cut inference costs about 90% and boosted coding speed.
stories.summary: Speaking at the AI Engineer conference in New York, Revolut's operations and infrastructure lead David Abitbol said the UK fintech cut AI coding inference costs by roughly 90% over less than a year. The company rolled out AI coding tools to about 2,000 engineers and moved its default to self-hosted Chinese open-weight models, GLM-5.1 and later GLM-5.3, served on 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs. He reported a 60% improvement in coding time and 70% in lead time. Revolut still uses other models such as Gemini or GPT for vision tasks, and Abitbol said privacy concerns apply mainly to APIs running outside China.
key_points: Revolut says self-hosting cut AI coding inference costs by about 90% compared with commercial services such as Claude.
The company reported a 60% improvement in coding time and 70% in lead time across roughly 2,000 engineers.
It runs GLM-5.3 on 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs and uses a model router for tasks such as vision.
Abitbol said the biggest gains came from debugging and ticket work rather than code generation alone.
He said long context windows were less useful than expected, with around 256,000 tokens being the practical sweet spot.
The figures are company claims made at a conference, not independently verified.

Global PC shipments fell 20.1% year on year in Q3 2026 to 62.7 million units, according to IDC. Neither the destination markets of China-built machines nor all details have been confirmed.

stories.headline: Graduates are managing AI - but are they learning much else?
stories.claim: Graduates are increasingly hired into AI-focused roles, raising questions about how much traditional professional skills they are learning.
stories.summary: The BBC looks at a new generation of graduates whose jobs centre on AI. Lotte Underwood, 25, is an AI associate at London PR agency Fight or Flight, managing around 30 AI agents, while Dillan Patel at engineering software firm Stride and Cian Clinton at consultancy Valliance also work heavily with AI tools. Employers such as ArvatoConnect say they want AI-focused graduates, and PwC's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer, based on 2.4 million US entry-level jobs, found AI-influenced entry roles are seven times more likely to require senior skills. Other firms, such as Portman Finance Group, say their graduate schemes still focus on learning the core trade. The piece questions whether the emphasis on AI leaves graduates short of traditional professional experience.
key_points: Lotte Underwood, 25, works as an AI associate at London PR agency Fight or Flight and spends more time managing AI agents than doing PR.
PwC's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer analysed 2.4 million US entry-level jobs and found AI-influenced roles are seven times more likely to need senior skills.
Entry-level roles with higher expectations have grown 35% since 2019, while other entry-level roles shrank by 10%, according to PwC.
ArvatoConnect has paused its usual graduate intake this year but plans to resume next year with a bigger AI focus.
Portman Finance Group says its two-year graduate scheme is built around learning the trade, with rotations across four areas.
PwC UK's Claire Reed says AI skills alone will not guarantee long-term career progression.

stories.headline: Democrats Sweep Republicans in Nearly Every Race That Matters
stories.claim: Democrats won key US midterm races on Tuesday, taking Senate seats and likely control of the House, a major setback for Trump.
stories.summary: Democrats performed strongly in the US midterm elections held on Tuesday 3 November, flipping seats in several places that Trump had won by double digits in 2024. In Texas, James Talarico beat Republican attorney general Ken Paxton in the Senate race, and Gina Hinojosa defeated Governor Greg Abbott, the first statewide Democratic win there since 1994. Democrats also took Senate seats in Kansas, South Carolina, Iowa and North Carolina, and held Georgia and New Hampshire, according to the Associated Press. White House sources blamed high petrol prices and cost of living tied to the Iran war, as well as immigration policy and candidate quality. Incoming House oversight chair Robert Garcia signalled an aggressive oversight push against the administration.
key_points: Democrats appear set to take the House and Senate after a strong night in battleground races across the US.
In Texas, Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, and Gina Hinojosa beat Governor Greg Abbott.
Democrats also won Senate races in Kansas, South Carolina, Iowa and North Carolina, according to the AP.
Trump officials blamed high gas prices and living costs linked to the Iran war, as well as immigration policy.
Republican redistricting plans backfired, with Democrats winning at least three redrawn seats in Florida and the North Carolina seat.

stories.market_take: A Democratic House and Senate could bring more policy gridlock and oversight pressure, which markets may weigh modestly.

stories.headline: Microsoft improves Windows 11 performance on 8 GB PCs as RAM prices keep climbing
stories.claim: Microsoft says it has made Windows 11 faster and more responsive on 8 GB PCs as memory prices rise.
stories.summary: Microsoft has announced performance changes to Windows 11 on PCs with 8 GB of RAM, as memory prices rise because of demand from AI data centres. The company claims such machines can be up to 20% more responsive and 40% faster at multitasking. Changes include keeping up to 2 GB more data in memory, faster Edge launches, Teams Efficiency Mode by default, Widgets loading only when used, and shorter Edge tab sleep times. Microsoft's commissioned benchmark found a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8 GB performed similarly to a 2021 model with 16 GB in selected tasks. The Register notes that Windows OEM and devices revenue fell 22% in the latest quarter, while overall profits rose.

Windows will keep up to 2 GB more active data in memory before using slower storage.

Microsoft's fiscal Q1 2027 adjusted earnings were $36.4 billion, up 18%, while Windows OEM and devices revenue fell 22%.
The Register suggests the changes are a way to help users stretch older hardware as memory prices rise.

The AI Security Institute received an extra £120M in the latest budget and recently regained access to new US AI models before release.

stories.headline: AMD on track to overtake Intel as biggest x86 outfit

Such a move would show how US policy on China technology can directly affect cloud and AI contracts. The story rests on a single report, and neither company's position is given in the summary.
key_points: The Financial Times reports that Oracle has abandoned a $7 billion AI deal with Tencent.
The decision is attributed to pressure from the Trump administration.
Reuters is carrying the story on the back of the FT report.
The summary gives no details on the deal's structure or timing.
No official comment from Oracle or Tencent is included in the summary.
stories.likelihood_reason: The FT is a highly reliable outlet, though the story is based on its own reporting and the companies have not confirmed it in this item.
signals: No official company confirmation in the summary
stories.market_take: Oracle may lose a sizeable AI cloud contract, while the episode highlights US-China tech risk.

stories.headline: Samsung’s Galaxy S27 Ultra may fix the privacy screen brightness flaw
stories.claim: Samsung's Galaxy S27 Ultra and S27 Pro may get a brighter privacy display, with a possible early-2027 launch.
stories.summary: Android Police, citing SamMobile, reports that the Galaxy S27 Ultra will get an upgraded Privacy Display that is brighter than the S26 Ultra's. The S27 Pro may also get the feature, which would be the first time Samsung offers it outside the Ultra line. Certification reportedly points to faster LPDDR6 memory and configurations up to 1TB for the S27 Pro, while the base model keeps LPDDR5X with up to 512GB. Samsung may announce the series in late January or early February 2027, about a month earlier than usual. Samsung has not confirmed any of these details.
key_points: SamMobile reports the S27 Ultra will have a brighter, upgraded Privacy Display than the S26 Ultra.
The S27 Pro may also include Privacy Display, which would be new for the non-Ultra range.
Certification reportedly suggests LPDDR6 memory and up to 1TB storage for the S27 Pro.
Renders reportedly show a rectangular camera island on the Pro and Ultra models.
Samsung may announce the series in late January or early February 2027, earlier than usual.
stories.likelihood_reason: Based on leaks and certification and third-party renders; SamMobile has a mixed record on specifics, and Samsung has not confirmed the details.
stories.market_take: Limited market effect; a possible boost for Samsung's display and memory suppliers if the specs are confirmed.

stocks.reason: A premium launch with better displays and memory could support sales if the rumours hold.
